newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - Market reaction to BoE rate rise.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Market reaction to BoE rate rise.

text.p: The Bank of England's newly independent monetary policy committee met for the first time this week and voted early Friday to raise its key interest rates by 0.25 percentage point to 6.50 percent.
Following are analysts' comments on the outlook for UK stocks, bonds and sterling.
NICK PARSONS, FOREIGN EXCHANGE STRATEGIST AT BANQUE PARIBAS:

"The rise is understandable and if they were going to raise rates it is best to do it early. There hasn't been a heavy move to sterling yet because of the U.S. payrolls but we're in for an extremely busy afternoon."
STEVE HANNAH, DIRECTOR OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH, IBJ:

"Sterling is going back up to 2.85 (marks) in the short term. This is not the last move in the tightening cycle. Sterling is proving attractive, not just because of the significant differentials against Germany but also because it is such an obvious EMU hedge. It's hard to see what will knock it off its perch."
NICK STAMENKOVIC, ECONOMIST AT DKB INTERNATIONAL:
"We could well be testing the highs (for sterling) we saw earlier this year."
JONATHAN YORK, FUTURES BROKER AT MEESPIERSON:
"The short end (short sterling) has come off a couple of ticks. I feel the market...at these sorts of levels is pretty fairly priced."
SIMON KNAPP, INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIST AT BZW:

"The uncertainty was about the timing rather than whether there would be a rate rise. They've got this rate rise out of the way, but the greater uncertainties about rates are towards the end of the year."
NICK KNIGHT, STOCK STRATEGIST AT NOMURA:
"It's no surprise and we need further rises. The market is in a strange mind set. Had they not (raised rates), the market would have felt they were mucking it up."
"This is a vote of confidence by the market that the central bankers are being proactive rather than reactive and that they know what they're doing."
MIKE DICKS, UK ECONOMIST AT LEHMAN BROTHERS:
"It is what we expected. The Bank is demonstrating its independence, trying to build its credibility and ensure that they will not be taking risks with inflation."

"It is clear the Bank of England has decided not to wait for the Chancellor's budget. They have decided to establish credibility early on and they have been consistent with their earlier policy advice." -- Joanne Russell, London Newsroom +44171 542 7708
